section.title: The Song of Moses
section.sectionRationale: Israel's first act on the far side of the sea is worship in song. This poem, among the oldest in Scripture, turns the crossing into theology: it names who God is, what He has done, and where He is taking His people, becoming the pattern for how the redeemed remember their redemption.
section.thesis: Freshly delivered from Egypt, Israel sings that the LORD is a warrior who has triumphed gloriously, unmatched among the gods, whose loving devotion will lead His redeemed people to His own holy dwelling, and Miriam leads the women in the same refrain.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the opening praise of the LORD as strength and salvation; the destruction of Pharaoh's army retold as poetry; the incomparable holiness of God; the promise that the nations will tremble while God brings His people to His mountain; and Miriam's answering song.

units.label: The LORD is my strength and my song
units.note: praise for the horse and rider thrown into the sea

verses.text:
Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the LORD: 
“I will sing to the LORD, for He is {{exalted|highly exalted}}. The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea.
The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation. He is my God, and I will praise Him, my father's God, and I will exalt Him.
The LORD is a {{warrior|warrior}}, the LORD is His name.

units.label: The enemy destroyed
units.note: sank like a stone, like lead

verses.text: Pharaoh's chariots and army He has cast into the sea; the finest of his officers are drowned in the Red Sea.
The depths have covered them; they sank there like a stone.
Your right hand, O LORD, is majestic in power; Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy.
You overthrew Your adversaries by Your great majesty. You unleashed Your burning wrath; it consumed them like stubble.
At the blast of Your nostrils the waters piled up; like a wall the currents stood firm; the depths congealed in the heart of the sea.
The enemy declared, ‘I will pursue, I will overtake. I will divide the spoils; I will gorge myself on them. I will draw my sword; my hand will destroy them.’
But You blew with Your breath, and the sea covered them. They sank like lead in the mighty waters.

units.label: Who is like You, O LORD

verses.text: Who among the gods is like You, O LORD? Who is like You, majestic in {{holiness|holiness}}, revered with praises, performing wonders?
You stretched out Your right hand, and the earth swallowed them up.
With loving devotion You will lead the people You have redeemed; with Your strength You will guide them to Your holy dwelling.

units.label: The nations tremble, the sanctuary promised

verses.text: The nations will hear and tremble; anguish will grip the dwellers of Philistia.
Then the chiefs of Edom will be dismayed; trembling will seize the leaders of Moab; those who dwell in Canaan will melt away,
and terror and dread will fall on them. By the power of Your arm they will be as still as a stone until Your people pass by, O LORD, until the people You have bought pass by.
You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance, the place, O LORD, You have prepared for Your dwelling, the sanctuary, O Lord, Your hands have established.
The LORD will reign forever and ever!”
For when Pharaoh's horses, chariots, and horsemen went into the sea, the LORD brought the waters of the sea back over them. But the Israelites walked through the sea on dry ground.
Then Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing.

And Miriam sang back to them: 
“Sing to the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and rider He has thrown into the sea.”

exalted.gloss: To be highly exalted, to triumph gloriously, to rise up in majesty. The very first word of Israel's worship after the crossing is a declaration that God alone has done this, He has triumphed, not Israel.

warrior.gloss: A man of war, a warrior. Israel does not sing that God helped them fight; He alone fought while they stood still, and this song names Him plainly as the warrior whose name is the LORD.

holiness.gloss: Holiness, set-apartness, the very otherness of God. The song's central question, who is like You, majestic in holiness, has no rival answer; God's holiness is what makes Him utterly incomparable among every so-called god of the nations.

basic.context: The moment Israel is safely across the sea, they burst into song, one of the oldest poems in the Bible. It retells what just happened, God alone destroying Pharaoh's army, and looks ahead to God bringing His redeemed people all the way to His holy mountain.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real song sung by real people at a specific moment of deliverance; it is poetry, using vivid images like the earth swallowing the enemy, but it describes an actual historical rescue. Its purpose is worship and remembrance, teaching every later reader how to respond rightly to God's saving power.
basic.originalLanguages: The song opens declaring God ga'ah, highly exalted, triumphant, crediting Him alone with the victory. It calls Him ish milchamah, a warrior, plainly and without embarrassment. And its central, unanswerable question asks who is like the LORD in qodesh, holiness, His utter set-apartness from every false god.
basic.typology: The song's hope, that God will bring His redeemed people to His own dwelling place, anticipates the whole biblical trajectory toward a people finally and fully at home with God, fulfilled ultimately in the new creation where God dwells with His people forever, Revelation 21:3.
basic.christ: Revelation 15:3 pictures the redeemed in heaven singing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb together, joining this ancient victory song to the greater and final victory won by Christ, the true and better warrior who triumphs not with a sword but through the cross.
basic.god: God is revealed here as both warrior and shepherd in the same breath, utterly holy and yet leading His people with loving devotion toward His own home. His incomparability is not an abstract claim but is proven by an act every Israelite there had just witnessed with their own eyes.
basic.crossReferences: Revelation 15:3-4 has the redeemed sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb together. Psalm 77:11-20 recalls this same crossing to strengthen faith in a later generation. Isaiah 12 echoes this song's language of the LORD as strength, song, and salvation.
basic.oneStory: Israel's first response to salvation is not relief alone but worship in song, retelling what God has done and trusting Him for what is still ahead. This pattern, redemption answered with praise that looks forward to God's dwelling with His people, runs to Revelation, where the redeemed sing this very song beside the song of the Lamb.

context.literary:
The song stands at a hinge in Exodus. Chapters 1 to 14 are prose, the long story of bondage, plagues and the night of escape, and chapter 14 closes by saying that the people 'feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses,' Exodus 14:31. Chapter 15 is what that belief sounds like. The book pauses its narrative and lets Israel answer in poetry before the wilderness journey begins in verse 22.

The poem has a clear shape. After the opening confession of verses 1 to 3, it falls into stanzas that each close on a simile of stone or weight. The drowned army sinks 'like a stone,' verse 5; the enemy sinks 'like lead,' verse 10; and the nations of Canaan will be 'as still as a stone until Your people pass by,' verse 16. The repeated image ties the past victory to the future one: the same power that sank Egypt will freeze every enemy on the road ahead.

The tenses move with the argument. Verses 1 to 12 look back on what the LORD has done. Verse 13 turns to what He will do, and verses 14 to 17 look forward to the nations, the mountain and the sanctuary. The song ends in verse 18 with no past or future limit at all: 'The LORD will reign forever and ever!'

The poet is also fond of contrast. The enemy's boast in verse 9 is a breathless run of first person verbs, I will pursue, overtake, divide, gorge, draw, destroy. Verse 10 answers it with a single breath from God, and the sea covers them. Human arrogance speaks six times; God acts once.

Verses 19 to 21 return to prose to restate the event, then close with Miriam's refrain, which repeats the first line of the song. That repetition frames the whole poem, so the song begins and ends on the horse and rider thrown into the sea.
context.historical:
The song celebrates the destruction of the most feared military technology of its day. Egypt's strength lay in its chariot corps, and Exodus has already stressed Pharaoh's six hundred choice chariots, Exodus 14:7. The 'finest of his officers' in verse 4 translates a word related to the number three, often explained as the third man who rode in a chariot crew as an officer or shield bearer. The song takes the pride of the empire and sinks it.

The Hebrew of the poem shows marks of great age, such as an old pronoun ending meaning 'them' that recurs from verse 5 to verse 17, and scholars of many schools treat it as one of the oldest poems in the Bible. Its language of God as a warrior riding over the waters would also have sounded pointed against the religions of the region. In Canaanite myth the storm god Baal fought and subdued Yam, the Sea, as a rival deity. Exodus 15 has no such battle with the sea. The waters are not an enemy god but an instrument in the LORD's hand; He piles them up with a breath and drops them again.

The second half looks toward peoples Israel had not yet met: Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan, verses 14 and 15. Forty years later those very nations would stand on Israel's route, and Rahab of Jericho would confess that the report of the Red Sea had made her people's courage fail, Joshua 2:9-11.

Miriam's tambourine belongs to a known custom. Women went out with tambourines and dancing to greet a victory, as Jephthah's daughter did, Judges 11:34, and as the women of Israel did for Saul and David, 1 Samuel 18:6-7. Here the custom is turned toward God alone; no human hero is praised.
context.canonical:
The song becomes the fountain of a whole stream of later worship. Its central confession, 'The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation,' verse 2, is sung again word for word in Psalm 118:14, and Isaiah 12:2 puts it in the mouth of the people who will sing on the day of a new exodus. Psalm 118 even picks up the song's 'right hand of the LORD' three times, Psalm 118:15-16.

The question of verse 11, 'Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?', echoes through Israel's prayers: Psalm 86:8, 'there is none like You among the gods,' and Micah 7:18, 'Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity?' Micah goes further. In Exodus the enemy is thrown into the sea; in Micah 7:19 God will 'cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea.' The song's image of judgment becomes an image of forgiveness. Nehemiah 9:11 recalls the pursuers hurled into the depths 'like a stone.'

The prophets use the crossing as the pattern for future rescue. Isaiah 51:10 asks, 'Was it not You who dried up the sea... who made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over?' and promises that the ransomed will return to Zion with singing. Psalm 78:54 describes the fulfilment of verse 17: 'He brought them to His holy land, to the mountain His right hand had acquired.'

The New Testament reads the crossing as a baptism, 1 Corinthians 10:1-2, and Luke calls the death and resurrection of Jesus His 'departure,' Luke 9:31, using the word exodos. The Bible's last book closes the circle. Beside a sea of glass the victors sing 'the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb,' Revelation 15:2-3, a new song whose words gather the themes of this one: the works of God are great, and He alone is holy.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to learn how to remember. A rescue that is not sung is soon forgotten, and Psalm 106:12-13 records exactly that danger: 'Then they believed His promises and sang His praise. Yet they soon forgot His works.' The song fixes the meaning of the event in the people's mouths, so that every retelling gives the glory to one actor.

He also wanted Israel to see that the victory at the sea was the first installment of a larger promise. The song does not stop at the far shore. It moves on to guidance, verse 13, to the nations on the road, verses 14 to 16, and to the sanctuary on God's mountain, verse 17. The redeemed are taught to read their present rescue as a pledge of the whole journey.

Finally, he meant them to know God by name and by character. 'The LORD is His name,' verse 3, and His name is bound up with what He does: He is majestic in holiness, He performs wonders, He redeems and buys a people, and He reigns. A people about to face thirst, hunger and enemies were given a song that told them who was leading them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The song records Israel's praise; it is not a law. Nothing in it commands believers to celebrate the death of enemies, and its warfare language describes the LORD's own action, not a model for human violence. Israel was told to stand still while He fought, Exodus 14:14.

What carries forward is the pattern. God's saving acts call for an answer of praise that names Him specifically, credits Him alone, and looks ahead in hope. The later Scriptures commend exactly this, from Psalm 118 to Revelation 15. The song also shows that worship can be corporate and led: Moses and Israel sing together, and Miriam leads the women in answering song. The church's singing of what God has done in Christ stands in this line, with the cross and resurrection as its great act.

debates.question: How should the song's celebration over the drowned Egyptian army be read?

views.label: Righteous joy in God's justice
views.case: The song celebrates God's judgment on an oppressor who had ordered Israel's baby boys thrown into the Nile, Exodus 1:22, and who pursued a freed people to destroy them, verse 9. Joy at the end of such cruelty is not bloodthirst. Revelation 15:3-4 has the redeemed praise God because His righteous acts have been revealed.

views.label: Praise held together with sorrow
views.case: Others stress that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 33:11, and that the song's joy is directed at God's rescue, not at human suffering as such. Christians read it alongside Jesus, who wept over the coming judgment of Jerusalem, Luke 19:41-44.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm the song's claim that God rightly judges oppression and rightly saves His people. The song's focus on God rather than on the dead Egyptians guides how that truth is voiced today: rejoicing in justice without delighting in destruction.

debates.question: What is the 'holy dwelling' and 'mountain of Your inheritance' in verses 13 and 17?

views.label: Mount Sinai
views.case: Israel's next great destination is the mountain of God, where Moses had already been told Israel would worship, Exodus 3:12. Some read verse 13 as pointing first to Sinai, where God will dwell among them in the tabernacle.

views.label: The land of Canaan as a whole
views.case: Verse 17 speaks of planting the people on the mountain of God's inheritance after the nations of Canaan have been passed, which suits the hill country of the promised land. Psalm 78:54 calls the land 'His holy land, to the mountain His right hand had acquired.'

views.label: Mount Zion and the temple
views.case: The words 'sanctuary' and 'the place You have prepared for Your dwelling' are later used of the Jerusalem temple; Solomon speaks of 'a place for You to dwell forever,' 1 Kings 8:13. On this reading the song looks ahead prophetically to Zion, which some take as evidence that the song was shaped over time.

debates.bearing: The song seems to see the whole journey in one view, from the mountain where God first meets them to the land where He plants them and the place He chooses to dwell. The New Testament carries the same hope further, to the city where God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3.

study.originalLanguages:
The song begins with the word ashirah, 'I will sing,' from shir, and the noun shirah, 'song,' gives the poem its traditional name. In verse 2 a different word appears, 'my song,' zimrat, usually taken from the root zamar, to make music, which is behind mizmor, the word for many titled psalms, though some connect it with a similar root meaning strength or protection. The line joins it to a short form of the divine name, Yah, the same element heard at the end of hallelujah. And 'salvation' is yeshuah, from the root yasha, to save, the root in the names Joshua and Jesus, whose name was given 'because He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21.

Verse 2 also has a verb that translators handle differently: 'I will praise Him,' anvehu. Some connect it with a root meaning to beautify or adorn, so 'I will glorify Him.' Others connect it with naveh, a dwelling or pasture, so 'I will make Him a habitation.' The second reading is attractive because verse 13 uses that very noun for God's 'holy dwelling,' neveh qodshekha. Either way the song begins and ends in the language of God's dwelling place.

The account of the sea is soaked in the vocabulary of breath. 'At the blast of Your nostrils,' verse 8, is literally the ruach of God's nostrils, and 'You blew with Your breath,' verse 10, uses ruach again. It is the same word as the 'strong east wind' of Exodus 14:21, and the word used of the Spirit of God over the waters in Genesis 1:2. The 'depths' of verses 5 and 8 are tehomot, the plural of tehom, 'the deep,' in Genesis 1:2. The poet describes the crossing as a new act of creation, God's breath dividing the deep so that dry land appears.

Verse 11 asks mi khamokha, 'Who is like You?', and asks it twice. The phrase is built into the name Michael, 'who is like God?' The 'wonders' God performs are pele, the word behind 'Wonderful' in Isaiah 9:6. Holiness, qodesh, is here paired with majesty, the verb adar, 'glorious,' also used of His right hand in verse 6.

Three words in verses 13 to 16 describe what God has done for Israel. 'Loving devotion' is chesed, covenant loyalty, as the BSB footnote explains. 'Redeemed' is gaal, the verb of the kinsman redeemer who buys back a relative from slavery, and it was first promised in Exodus 6:6. And 'the people You have bought,' verse 16, uses qanah, to acquire or purchase, the verb Moses later uses when he calls God Israel's 'Father and Creator,' Deuteronomy 32:6. Psalm 74:2 joins the ideas: 'Your congregation, which You purchased long ago and redeemed.'

Verse 17 speaks of the place God has 'prepared' for His 'dwelling,' makon leshivtekha, literally 'a fixed place for Your sitting,' the throne language that Solomon echoes at the temple dedication, 1 Kings 8:13. God is pictured not only as a warrior but as a king taking His seat. That is why the song ends, 'The LORD will reign,' yimlokh, verse 18.

In verse 20 Miriam is called nevi'ah, 'the prophetess,' the first woman to bear the title in Scripture. The instrument she takes up is the toph, a hand drum or tambourine.

typology.type: Israel's passage through the sea, Exodus 15:19
typology.fulfillment: Paul says Israel 'passed through the sea' and 'were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,' 1 Corinthians 10:1-2. The crossing was a passage from slavery to freedom through waters of death, with the enemy left behind. Christian baptism marks a greater passage, union with Christ in His death and resurrection, Romans 6:3-4, and freedom from a stronger master, sin itself. The type falls short, as Paul warns in 1 Corinthians 10:5: most who passed through the sea still perished in the wilderness, so the outward sign never saves without faith.

The LORD fights while His people stand still, Exodus 14:14. Christ fights the same way for His people, alone and on their behalf, but His victory comes through His own death. At the cross He disarmed the powers and 'made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross,' Colossians 2:15. Revelation pictures the final campaign: the rider called Faithful and True 'judges and wages war' with righteousness, Revelation 19:11. The escalation is that the enemy defeated is not an empire but sin, death and the devil, and the warrior Himself bears the wound.

typology.type: The redeemed, purchased people, Exodus 15:13 and 15:16
typology.fulfillment: God redeems Israel as a kinsman buys back a relative from slavery, and He 'bought' them for Himself. The New Testament uses the same pictures for the church: believers were redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:18-19, and the Lamb is praised because 'by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe,' Revelation 5:9. The price in Exodus was the judgment on Egypt and the Passover lamb; in Christ the price is the Redeemer's own life, and the people bought come from every nation.

typology.type: The sanctuary God's hands established, Exodus 15:17
typology.fulfillment: The song ends with God planting His people on His mountain around His sanctuary. That hope took shape in the tabernacle and the temple, but both were made with human hands and both could be left or destroyed. Jesus spoke of His body as the temple, John 2:19-21, and told His disciples He was going 'to prepare a place for you,' John 14:2-3, an echo of the place God prepared in verse 17. The final fulfilment is a city with no temple, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22.

typology.type: The song of victory beside the sea, Exodus 15:1
typology.fulfillment: Israel sang on the shore with the enemy dead behind them. John sees the conquerors standing beside a sea of glass mixed with fire, holding harps, singing 'the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb,' Revelation 15:2-3. The correspondence is deliberate, but the escalation is vast: the victory is over the beast, the singers come from all nations, and the song praises God as 'King of the nations.' Israel's song was soon followed by grumbling, verse 24; the final song will never be interrupted.

study.christ:
The song leads to Christ first by the words it gives. Its key term is yeshuah, salvation, and its confession, 'He has become my salvation,' verse 2, is the confession the church makes about the one named Jesus, 'because He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21. Psalm 118 sings the same line, Psalm 118:14, and the same psalm supplies the crowd's cry at the triumphal entry, 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord,' Psalm 118:26 and Matthew 21:9. The words of the sea song are on the road into Jerusalem.

It leads to Christ by pattern. At the transfiguration Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about His 'departure,' Luke 9:31, the word exodos. The death and resurrection of Jesus are His exodus, the decisive act by which God brings a people out of bondage. Paul calls Christ 'our Passover lamb,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and describes Israel's passage through the sea as a baptism, 1 Corinthians 10:1-2. The deliverance this song celebrates is the template the apostles use to explain the cross.

It leads to Christ by contrast. The warrior of Exodus 15 fights from outside the battle, with wind and water, and the enemy dies. The warrior of the gospel enters the battle in human flesh and dies Himself, and by that death destroys 'him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil,' Hebrews 2:14. The song's right hand shatters the enemy, verse 6; the hands of Christ are pierced, and in that weakness He triumphs over the powers, Colossians 2:15.

It also leads to Christ by the goal it names. The song's hope is that God will bring His people into His dwelling. Jesus goes ahead 'to prepare a place for you' and promises to 'welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am,' John 14:2-3. In Him the dwelling of God has already come among His people, John 1:14.

And the song reaches Christ in the end by being sung again. The victors of Revelation 15 sing 'the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb,' Revelation 15:3. The two songs are not rivals; the first was always pointing toward the second. We should not force every image of the poem onto Jesus, the horse and rider, Philistia and Edom are part of Israel's history, but the song itself sets the direction the New Testament follows: salvation by God's own hand, through death, leading to His presence and His reign.
study.god:
The song's first claim about God is that He acts alone. The subject of almost every verb in verses 1 to 12 is the LORD, and Israel does nothing but walk through. He is 'a warrior,' verse 3, yet the next words are 'the LORD is His name.' His name is not a title He shares; it is the name He revealed at the bush, Exodus 3:14-15, and the song says that the God of the burning bush is the God who fought at the sea.

He is incomparable. The question 'Who among the gods is like You?', verse 11, is not an admission that other gods are real rivals but a verdict after a contest. The plagues were judgments 'against all the gods of Egypt,' Exodus 12:12, and Jethro will draw the conclusion, 'Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods,' Exodus 18:11. God's uniqueness is shown in holiness, in the praise He deserves, and in wonders no one else can perform.

He holds wrath and love together. Verse 7 speaks of His 'burning wrath' consuming the enemy like stubble, and verse 13 speaks of His chesed, His covenant love, leading His people. These are not two moods but one faithful character. The same act that ends the oppressor rescues the oppressed, and the same breath that piles up the waters for Israel lets them fall on Pharaoh.

He is Creator as well as Redeemer. The breath over the deep, the dry ground in the midst of the sea and the command of the waters all recall Genesis 1. God does not merely win a battle; He remakes a world for His people to walk through.

He is the God who dwells and reigns. The song moves from His arm to His dwelling, from the battlefield to the sanctuary, and ends with His endless kingship, verse 18. His purpose in saving is not only to remove Israel from Egypt but to bring them to Himself, as He will say at Sinai, 'I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself,' Exodus 19:4.

For worship, the song teaches that praise should be specific and personal. 'He is my God, and I will praise Him, my father's God, and I will exalt Him,' verse 2. Israel sings what God has done, who He is, and what He has promised, and every generation of believers is invited to do the same with the greater salvation it has seen.

crossReferences.note: The prose command behind the song. Moses tells the terrified people to stand firm and see the LORD's salvation, because 'The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.' The song's picture of God as the only warrior, verse 3, is the poetic answer to that promise now kept.

Repeats Exodus 15:2 word for word, 'The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation,' and then celebrates the right hand of the LORD three times, echoing Exodus 15:6. A later worshipper takes the sea song as his own after a new rescue.

Isaiah places the same confession in the mouth of the people on the day God gathers them again: 'the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and He also has become my salvation.' The first exodus song becomes the song of the promised second exodus.

A sober commentary on this chapter. 'Then they believed His promises and sang His praise. Yet they soon forgot His works.' The psalm shows how quickly the song gave way to grumbling, which is exactly what happens at Marah only three days later, Exodus 15:24.

Rahab tells the spies that the fear of Israel has fallen on Jericho and that hearts have melted since hearing how the LORD dried up the Red Sea. The prophecy of Exodus 15:14-16, that the dwellers of Canaan would melt away in terror, is heard coming true from Canaanite lips.

Micah asks the song's question, 'Who is a God like You?', and answers it with forgiveness. As Pharaoh's army was thrown into the sea, so God 'will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea.' The judgment image of Exodus 15:4-5 becomes a picture of pardon.

The prophet calls on the arm of the LORD to wake as in days of old, recalling the God 'who made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over.' The exodus becomes the pattern for the return from exile, with the ransomed entering Zion with singing.

Describes the fulfilment of Exodus 15:13-17. God led His people like a flock, the sea engulfed their enemies, and 'He brought them to His holy land, to the mountain His right hand had acquired.' The song's future tense becomes the psalm's past tense.

Paul says the forefathers all passed through the sea and were baptized into Moses, yet with most of them God was not pleased. The crossing celebrated in Exodus 15 becomes a picture of baptism and a warning that the redeemed must persevere in faith.

Moses himself appears with Elijah and speaks with Jesus about the departure, exodos, He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. The man who led Israel's song at the sea discusses the greater exodus of the cross and resurrection.

The conquerors stand beside a sea of glass and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Its lines, 'Who will not fear You, O Lord?' and 'You alone are holy,' echo Exodus 15:11, and the nations who trembled in Exodus 15:14 now come to worship.

Hannah's song borrows the sea song's great question: 'There is no one holy like the LORD... there is no Rock like our God.' Like Exodus 15 it celebrates God's reversal of the proud and the weak, and it in turn shapes Mary's song in Luke 1:46-55.

study.oneStory:
Genesis ended with Israel in Egypt, and Exodus opened with the family of promise enslaved and its sons thrown into the Nile. The question hanging over those chapters was whether God would remember His covenant with Abraham, Exodus 2:24. The Song of Moses is the answer sung aloud. The God of the fathers, 'my father's God,' verse 2, has kept His word.

The song also answers something older. The language of breath over the deep and dry land appearing takes the reader back to Genesis 1. In a world spoiled by sin and ruled by a tyrant, God acts again as Creator, making a way through the waters and forming a people for Himself. The fall had driven humanity out of God's presence; the goal of this rescue is to bring a people back in, to His holy dwelling, verse 13.

What the song sets up is the rest of the Old Testament's hope. Israel will be led, fed and given water in the wilderness, brought to Sinai, and then to the land where God will plant them and build His sanctuary. The prophets, when the nation fails and goes into exile, will reach back to this song and promise a new exodus with new singing, Isaiah 12 and Isaiah 51. The pattern is set: God saves, His people sing, and the song looks forward to His dwelling among them.

That pattern comes to its centre in Christ. He accomplishes His exodus at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31, defeats the enemy through His own death, and gathers a people redeemed with His blood from every nation, Revelation 5:9. Believers now live between the crossing and the arrival, like Israel on the far shore, singing already while the journey is still ahead.

The story ends where the song ends, with the LORD reigning forever. In the new creation 'the sea was no more,' Revelation 21:1, the waters of chaos and judgment gone, and God's dwelling is with humanity, Revelation 21:3. Beside the sea of glass the redeemed sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb, and the question of Exodus 15:11 receives its final answer from every nation: no one is like Him.

quiz.q: What does the opening line of the song credit to the LORD?

options.text: That He is highly exalted, having thrown the horse and rider into the sea.
options.note: Verse 1 gives this exact confession; the victory belongs to God alone.

options.text: That Israel's own military skill won the day.
options.note: The song explicitly credits the LORD, not Israel's own strength or strategy.

options.text: That Moses personally defeated Pharaoh's army.
options.note: Moses leads the song, but the praise is directed to the LORD, not to Moses as a warrior.

options.text: That the Egyptians simply retreated on their own.
options.note: The song describes decisive divine destruction of the army, not a voluntary retreat.

quiz.q: How does the song describe the LORD in verse 3?

options.text: As a warrior, whose name is the LORD.
options.note: The Hebrew names Him plainly, ish milchamah, a man of war, a warrior.

options.text: As a distant judge uninvolved in the battle.
options.note: The song's whole point is God's active, personal involvement in the fight.

options.text: As merely an advisor to Moses.
options.note: The song presents God as the one who actually fought and won, not a passive advisor.

options.text: The song gives no description of God's character.
options.note: Verse 3 explicitly describes Him as a warrior.

quiz.q: What unanswered question forms the heart of the song's praise in verse 11?

options.text: Who among the gods is like You, O LORD, majestic in holiness?
options.note: This rhetorical question asserts God's total incomparability among every rival power.

options.text: Who will lead Israel into the promised land?
options.note: That question is answered elsewhere; verse 11's question is about God's unmatched holiness and power.

options.text: Why did Pharaoh pursue Israel?
options.note: The song is not asking why Pharaoh pursued; it is praising God's incomparable character.

options.text: The song contains no rhetorical questions.
options.note: Verse 11 is explicitly framed as a question with an assumed answer, no one.

quiz.q: What does the song anticipate God doing for His people in verses 13 and 17?

options.text: Leading them with loving devotion to His own holy dwelling place.
options.note: These verses look ahead to God bringing Israel to His sanctuary, His holy mountain.

options.text: Abandoning them once they crossed the sea.
options.note: The opposite is promised; God will lead and guide them onward with loving devotion.

options.text: Returning them to slavery in Egypt.
options.note: The song looks forward to the promised land, not a return to bondage.

options.text: No future hope is expressed in the song.
options.note: Verses 13 and 17 explicitly express forward-looking hope and promise.

quiz.q: Who leads the women in an answering refrain at the end of the passage?

options.text: Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, with a tambourine.
options.note: Verse 20 names her directly and describes her leading role in the worship.

options.text: Zipporah, the wife of Moses.
options.note: The text names Miriam, not Zipporah, as the one leading the women's song.

options.text: Aaron himself leads the women in song.
options.note: The text specifically credits Miriam, described as a prophetess, with leading the women.

options.text: No one leads a second song; the passage ends after verse 18.
options.note: Verses 20 to 21 explicitly describe Miriam's separate, answering refrain.

questions: Israel's first act of freedom was worship, not planning or complaining. What is the first thing you tend to do after God clearly answers a hard prayer, and does it look like this song?
The song credits the LORD alone for the victory, refusing to let Israel take any glory for themselves. Where are you tempted to take credit for something that was really God's work in your life?
The unanswered question, 'who is like You, majestic in holiness,' assumes there is no rival. What false gods, however subtle, compete for that place of incomparable trust in your own life?

The song looks forward in hope even while still fresh from crisis, trusting God to finish what He started. What situation in your life needs that same forward-looking trust rather than just relief that today's danger has passed?
Miriam led the women in their own refrain, a whole community joining the same worship together. Who could you bring alongside you this week to praise God together for something He has done?

translationNotes.note: My father's God echoes the covenant language used with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, tying this new act of salvation to God's much older promises to the patriarchs.
The blast of Your nostrils is vivid poetic imagery for God's powerful breath or wind, matching the historical description of the strong east wind in Exodus 14:21.

The mountain of Your inheritance likely refers to the land of Canaan broadly, or Mount Zion specifically as its later center of worship, though this song was composed before either the conquest or the building of the temple.
